resolute

/REZ-uh-loot/ - the stress falls on REZ · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Resolute means firm and determined; refusing to waver.

Three hours of cross-examination could not shake the witness; she remained resolute, repeating her account without changing a single detail.

Example

Doctors told Ruy he might never run again; he circled the date of the village's spring footrace on the calendar anyway. Through a second surgery, missed milestones, and therapists urging him to settle for walking, he stayed resolute - and crossed the finish line in May, last and beaming.

Resolute describes firmness about a decision already made: the mind is set, and pressure, mockery, or delay will not move it. It praises steadiness of purpose rather than energy or effort.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

steadfast: Steadfast praises loyalty that holds steady over time — the friend still beside you in year ten, the ally who never drifts. Resolute points at one decision: the mind is made up, and pressure will not reopen it. Steadfast is proven across years; resolute is proven the moment pressure arrives.

unwavering: Unwavering describes the visible surface of firmness — no flicker, no hesitation, nothing bending at any point. Resolute names what sits underneath: a decision already made and closed to argument. A rehearsed voice can sound unwavering; only someone who has genuinely settled the choice is resolute.

firm: Firm is the everyday, all-purpose word for holding a position — a firm offer, a firm handshake, a firm no. Resolute is stronger and more admiring: the decision is settled and will not bend under real pressure. A firm answer holds for now; a resolute one has closed the question.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

wavering: swinging between choices

indecisive: unable to settle on a course

Where it sits · how completely the decision resists reopening — determined → resolute → immovable

determined vs. resolute: Determined says you truly intend to do it; resolute goes further - the decision is settled, and pressure will not reopen it.

immovable vs. resolute: Immovable outdoes resolute: the resolute negotiator holds her position through every argument, while an immovable one will not even return to the table to hear a new offer.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — re-

Prefix — re-: thoroughly, back

Root — solute

Root — solute: loosened, settled (from Latin solvere)

Put it together

Put it together: Re- (thoroughly) + solute (loosened, settled) = thoroughly settled. Latin resolvere meant 'to loosen completely' - and a question fully loosened is a question settled. A resolute person has settled the question inside themselves, once and for all. You will meet the parent verb, resolve, later in this unit's reading.

Use the root in a new word: dissolve

Use the root in a new word: dissolve: Sugar will dissolve in warm tea, loosening apart until nothing solid remains.

Word Building

Word Choice

formal, admiring

Resolute praises a made-up mind. Its neighbors in this unit divide the ground: indomitable says no defeat can discourage you, and assiduous says your careful effort never flags - resolute says your decision will not bend. It is admiring where 'stubborn' is critical; if the firmness looks unreasonable, English reaches for stubborn instead.
